title: How to Retire Using a Two-Phase Income Strategy (Pre-62 and Post-62)
description: Building a 'Bridge' plan for early retirees before Social Security kicks in.
content:
Retirement is rarely a flat line of income. For most Americans—especially those retiring before age 65—it is a tale of two cities. Phase 1 is the 'Bridge Phase' (retirement date to age 62/65/70), where you are 100% reliant on your own savings to pay the bills and buy health insurance. Phase 2 is the 'Guaranteed Income Phase,' where Social Security and Medicare significantly lower your portfolio burden. Failing to separate these phases often leads to over-saving for Phase 2 while under-saving for Phase 1. This guide explains how to structure your assets to cross the bridge safely.

Key Takeaways

  • The Expensive Decade: The years between 55 and 65 are often the most expensive of your life due to travel ('Go-Go years') and private health insurance premiums. You need a specific 'Bridge Fund' for this.
  • Asset Spend-Down: In Phase 1, you aggressively spend down Taxable Brokerage accounts or Cash. This keeps your taxable income low, helping you qualify for ACA healthcare subsidies.
  • The Social Security Delay: By spending your own cash in Phase 1, you allow your Social Security benefit to grow by ~8% per year until age 70. You are essentially buying a larger government annuity.
  • Tax Bracket Arbitrage: Phase 1 is the perfect time for Roth Conversions. Since you have no wages and no Social Security income, you can fill up the 10% and 12% tax brackets with Roth conversions at a discount.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The ACA (Obamacare) 'Subsidy Cliff' is a major factor in Phase 1. By keeping your 'Modified Adjusted Gross Income' (MAGI) low during early retirement, you can save $10,000+ per year in health insurance premiums. This requires living off non-taxable sources like Cash or Roth principal.

The Two-Phase Budget

Scenario: Retiring at 55. Social Security at 70.

Phase 1: The Bridge (Age 55-70)

  • Expenses: $80,000/year (High travel + High insurance).
  • Income Source: 100% Portfolio Withdrawals.
  • Annual Draw: $80,000.
  • Duration: 15 Years.
  • Cash Needed: ~$1.2 Million (ignoring growth).

Phase 2: The Anchor (Age 70+)

  • Expenses: $70,000/year (Less travel + Medicare).
  • Income Source: Social Security ($45,000) + Portfolio ($25,000).
  • Annual Draw: Only $25,000.
  • Risk Profile: Extremely Safe. Your portfolio withdrawals dropped by 68%.

The Lesson: You don't need a portfolio that supports $80k forever. You need a portfolio that supports $80k for 15 years, and then $25k forever.

Execution Tactics

  1. Separate the Buckets: Physically separate the 'Bridge' money (Cash/Bonds) from the 'Core' retirement money (Stocks). Seeing the Bridge account drain to zero by age 70 is the plan, not a failure.
  2. Roth Conversion Window: From age 60 to 70, you have no wages and no RMDs. Convert Traditional IRA to Roth up to the 22% bracket every year. This lowers your RMDs at age 73.
  3. Healthcare Engineering: In Phase 1, watch your income. Taking $100k from a Traditional IRA might cost you $15k in ACA subsidies. Taking $100k from a Taxable account (principal) counts as $0 income.
  4. Delay Claiming: Every year you delay Social Security is an 8% guaranteed, inflation-protected return. Spend your own bonds first to 'buy' this higher government bond.

Frequently Asked Questions

What if I run out of bridge money?

Claim Social Security early (62). It locks in a permanent reduction, but it solves cash flow. The Bridge Strategy carries the risk of market crashes depleting the bridge faster than expected.

Should I buy an annuity for Phase 2?

Social Security is your annuity. By delaying to 70, you maximize it. If that isn't enough, a QLAC (Qualified Longevity Annuity Contract) starting at 80 can act as insurance against living too long.

Is this 'Bucket Strategy'?

Yes, it is a time-based variation. Bucket 1 (Years 1-15) is spent down. Bucket 2 (Years 16+) is allowed to grow.
